section.title: Doing Good to All
section.sectionRationale: The life of the Spirit works itself out in community. The spiritual restore the fallen gently, carry one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ, while each also carries his own load before God. Paul warns that God is not mocked: we reap what we sow, whether to the flesh or to the Spirit. So believers must not grow weary in well-doing but do good to everyone, especially the household of faith.
section.thesis: Those who walk by the Spirit bear one another's burdens and so fulfill the law of Christ, testing their own work rather than comparing, for God is not mocked and each reaps what he sows; therefore believers must sow to the Spirit and never tire of doing good to all, especially to the family of faith.
section.frameNote: Three movements: restoring the fallen and bearing one another's burdens to fulfill the law of Christ; the sober principle that each reaps what he sows, to the flesh or to the Spirit; and the call not to grow weary but to do good to everyone, especially the household of faith.

units.label: Bear one another's burdens
units.note: restore the fallen and fulfill the law of Christ

verses.text: Brothers, if someone is caught in a trespass, you who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of {{prautes|gentleness}}. But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted.
Carry one another's {{baros|burdens}}, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.
If anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.
Each one should test his own work. Then he will have reason to boast in himself alone, and not in someone else.
For each one should carry his own load.
Nevertheless, the one who receives instruction in the word must share in all good things with his instructor.

units.label: You reap what you sow
units.note: to the flesh or to the Spirit

verses.text: Do not be deceived: God is not to be mocked. Whatever a man {{speiro|sows}}, he will reap in return.
The one who sows to please his flesh, from the flesh will reap destruction; but the one who sows to please the Spirit, from the Spirit will reap eternal life.
Let us not grow weary in well-doing, for in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up.
Therefore, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to the family of faith.

prautes.gloss: Gentleness, meekness, strength under control. It is one of the fruits of the Spirit, and here it is the spirit in which the spiritual are to restore a fallen brother, not with harshness or superiority but with tender, humble care, watchful of their own weakness. Gentleness marks the community shaped by the Spirit rather than by rivalry.

baros.gloss: A weight, a heavy burden too great to carry alone. Believers are to carry one another's baros, sharing the crushing loads of sin, sorrow, and struggle, and in doing so they fulfill the law of Christ, the law of love. This is distinct from the load each must carry in verse 5; the heavy burden is shared, the personal responsibility is owned.

speiro.gloss: To sow, to scatter seed. Paul draws on the farming truth that the harvest matches the seed: sow to the flesh and reap destruction, sow to the Spirit and reap eternal life. The word makes daily choices weighty, for each is a seed with a certain harvest, and God is not mocked, so the outcome is sure.

basic.context: Life in the Spirit is not private; it shapes how believers treat each other. Paul tells the spiritual to restore those who fall, gently and humbly, and to carry one another's heavy burdens, which fulfills the law of Christ. Yet each is also responsible before God for his own life. Then he gives a farming law of the soul: you reap what you sow. So keep sowing to the Spirit and never tire of doing good to all.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the Spirit filled life worked out in community. Read the seeming tension between bear one another's burdens and each carry his own load as two truths held together: shared support and personal responsibility. The sowing and reaping principle grounds everyday choices in eternal outcomes.
basic.originalLanguages: The fallen are to be restored with prautes, gentleness, a fruit of the Spirit. Believers carry one another's baros, heavy burdens, fulfilling the law of Christ. And the law of the harvest is stated with speiro, to sow: what you sow, to flesh or Spirit, you will reap.
basic.typology: The law of Christ, fulfilled in bearing burdens, is the law of love that Christ Himself embodied by bearing our burdens at the cross. Sowing and reaping echoes the wisdom of Scripture and points to the final harvest, the day of judgment and reward that runs through the whole Bible.
basic.christ: The law of Christ is the pattern of Jesus who bore our burdens and laid down His life in love. To carry one another's burdens is to walk in His way. The eternal life reaped by sowing to the Spirit is the life Christ secured and gives, the harvest of His finished work applied by the Spirit.
basic.god: God is not mocked: He sees and He is just, and the harvest of every life matches its sowing. He is the God who rewards persevering good and who gives eternal life to those who sow to the Spirit. His moral order is sure, so no one deceives Him and no good done in faith is wasted.
basic.crossReferences: John 13 gives the new command to love as Christ loved, the law of Christ. 2 Corinthians 9 develops sowing and reaping in generosity. James 5 speaks of restoring the wanderer.
basic.oneStory: The gospel creates a new community that lives by the Spirit and loves like Christ. Bearing burdens and doing good are the shape of the new creation life breaking into the present. The sure harvest points forward to the final day when God gathers the fruit of grace and gives eternal life.

context.literary:
Galatians 6:1-10 follows without a break from 5:25-26, where Paul closed the previous section with a warning against conceit, provoking and envy. The new section shows what the opposite looks like in practice. The pivot is the very first sentence. Someone is caught in a wrongdoing, and the question is how a church of people who have just been told to walk in step with the Spirit will treat him.

The passage looks like a string of loosely joined proverbs, and some readers have taken it that way, but there is a clear movement. Verses 1 to 5 deal with the inward life of the community, the way members treat one another's failures, their burdens and their self-estimate. Verse 6 turns to material sharing with teachers. Verses 7 to 10 widen into a principle of sowing and reaping and end with a summons to do good. The thread running through all of it is the community's care for its own members and then, in verse 10, for outsiders.

The verses 2 to 5 contain what looks like a contradiction. Verse 2 says to carry one another's burdens, and verse 5 says each one should carry his own load. Paul has placed the two statements close together on purpose, and the key is in the vocabulary, since the two words for burden and load are different. Verses 3 and 4 sit between them as a warning about self-deception and a call to self-examination.

The agricultural image in verses 7 to 9 is carefully built. Paul states the law of sowing and reaping, divides it into two fields, flesh and Spirit, and then gives the work a time frame, 'in due time,' that makes patience the hinge of the whole. The section prepares the ground for the final summary, which Paul writes in his own hand in 6:11.
context.historical:
A believer 'caught in a trespass' might have been someone who had slipped into one of the sins on Paul's list in 5:19-21, and in a young church made up of former pagans such falls were common. The question of how to handle them was not academic. The choices were harsh judgment, which the divided Galatian community was already prone to, or looking the other way. Paul asks for a third course: restoration done with gentleness by those who are walking in the Spirit.

The instruction to share good things with one's teacher in verse 6 reflects the way the early churches supported those who taught them. There were no professional pastors in the modern sense, and teachers could be wandering or settled, and they depended on the hospitality and giving of their students. Paul himself sometimes refused such support to avoid hindering the gospel, 1 Corinthians 9:12, yet he insisted that those who preach the gospel had the right to a living from it, 1 Corinthians 9:14.

The image of sowing and reaping was part of the life of everyone in the region. Farming was the foundation of the economy, and the saying that you reap what you sow was a proverb in Jewish and Greek culture alike. Such a saying could be used cynically, but Paul uses it to ground ethics in a law as certain as the seasons.

The phrase 'the household of faith' fits the way the early church understood itself. Churches met in homes and thought of themselves as a family. For those who had been cut off from relatives by their conversion, this language was a precious assurance. Paul's call to do good to everyone, with special attention to this household, also carried a practical edge in a time when Christians might be the poorest members of their cities and were remembered for caring for the poor, Galatians 2:10.
context.canonical:
The principle of sowing and reaping runs through the wisdom literature and the prophets. Job 4:8 says that those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same, Proverbs 22:8 that he who sows injustice will reap disaster, and Proverbs 11:18 that he who sows righteousness reaps a true reward. Hosea 8:7 puts it in sharper form, 'they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind,' and Hosea 10:12 invites Israel to sow righteousness and reap the fruit of loving devotion. The harvest also carries a note of hope, as in Psalm 126:5-6, where those who sow in tears reap with shouts of joy.

In the New Testament, Jesus uses the sower and seed image for the kingdom, Mark 4, and Paul uses it for giving in 2 Corinthians 9:6-8 and for the resurrection in 1 Corinthians 15:42-44. The idea of final reckoning appears in Romans 2:6-8 and 2 Corinthians 5:10, where each person receives his due. Paul's teaching on the harvest is not a separate doctrine but a standing way of speaking about the link between a life and its outcome.

The 'law of Christ' in verse 2 appears only here by that name, with a close relative in 1 Corinthians 9:21, where Paul says he is 'under the law of Christ.' It has its roots in Jesus' new command to love as He loved, John 13:34, and in the Sermon on the Mount's reworking of the law's demands, Matthew 5 to 7. Mutual burden bearing recalls Romans 15:1-3, where the strong are to bear with the weak because Christ did not please Himself. The call to restore wanderers finds its echo in Matthew 18:15 and James 5:19-20.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted the Galatians to see that the Spirit's work does not end in private piety but shows up in how a community handles the weakest moments of its members. A church that was biting and devouring, 5:15, could easily become a church that crushed the one who fell. Paul tells the spiritual to restore, and in the same sentence he tells them to keep watch on themselves.

He also wanted to guard against two opposite distortions. One is the pride that looks down on the fallen and believes it is something when it is nothing, verse 3. The other is the dependence that expects others to carry everything, which verse 5 rules out. By setting carrying one another's burdens beside carrying one's own load, he describes a community in which people help without taking over and are helped without giving up responsibility.

The sowing and reaping section was meant to sober them and to encourage them. The warning, 'God is not to be mocked,' is a serious one, directed at those who thought they could live as they liked, but the verses end with a promise: in due time they will reap, if they do not give up. Paul closes the section by turning the whole teaching into a daily habit, to do good to everyone as opportunity allows.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the passage is plainly prescriptive: restore, watch yourself, carry, test your work, share, do not grow weary, do good. These are commands to the church in every age. What requires care is the way they are applied. 'Restore' does not mean ignoring sin, and 'gentleness' does not mean softness about wrong. The word Paul uses for restoring implies mending something that is broken, and the broken thing is the person's walk with God.

The sowing and reaping statement is a principle, not a prediction about every circumstance. Paul does not say that every hardship is the direct result of the sufferer's own sowing, and the book of Job warns against reading life in that way. He describes the moral order that God has built into the world and the final outcome of two kinds of life. Reading it as a formula that explains every illness or failure would be a misuse.

The direction to share with one's teacher describes a practice that the church was asked to keep, but the form of the support will differ with the culture. What is not optional is the principle of generosity toward those who feed the church with the word.

debates.question: What is 'the law of Christ'?

views.label: The teaching and example of Jesus
views.case: The phrase points to the pattern Jesus set and commanded, especially the new commandment to love one another as He loved, John 13:34. Paul, who in 1 Corinthians 9:21 says he is under the law of Christ, seems to refer to a norm of life drawn from Christ's own words and way. Bearing burdens fits that: Christ bore ours.

views.label: The law of love that fulfils the Mosaic law
views.case: Others take it as Paul's way of speaking of the Mosaic law as fulfilled in love, Galatians 5:14, now in the hands of those who belong to Christ. The law is not abandoned but received through Christ and carried out by the Spirit, Romans 8:4.

views.label: A rhetorical counterpoint to the opponents' law
views.case: Some suggest Paul may be playing on the agitators' language, saying that those who want a law should be given one, and that it is the law of love that Christ has set in place. This reading is possible but cannot be proved.

debates.bearing: All three readings agree that the content of the law of Christ is self-giving love and that it is carried out in practical acts like burden-bearing. Paul does not bring back the Mosaic code under a new name, nor does he cut the Christian life loose from all norms.

debates.question: Does 'from the Spirit will reap eternal life' make eternal life a reward for good deeds?

views.label: A principle that fruit proves the root
views.case: Eternal life is the gift of God, Romans 6:23, received by faith, and the sowing to the Spirit is the evidence of that gift at work. Paul's point is that a life given to the Spirit reaches the end God intended, not that works purchase the end. Ephesians 2:8-10 sets grace and works in this order.

views.label: A real condition of final salvation
views.case: Some read the verse and parallel passages like Romans 2:6-8 as teaching that persevering in good is a necessary part of reaching eternal life, with God judging by works. Many who hold this still insist that the works are Spirit-given.

views.label: A sober warning with a promise
views.case: A third approach emphasises the double edge of the verse. It warns those who sow to the flesh and promises those who sow to the Spirit, without trying to say how each fits into the logic of justification.

debates.bearing: The letter as a whole rules out earning acceptance by works, Galatians 2:16 and 3:11, so the sowing principle must be read within the gospel of grace. It describes the life that grace produces and the destiny to which it leads.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verb in verse 1 can mean being overtaken or being caught, and many readers hear in it a surprise rather than deliberate rebellion. The wrongdoing is a 'trespass,' a word that means a stumble or false step, and the way Paul describes the person as caught in it implies someone who has slipped rather than someone who has set out to sin.

The verb for 'restore' is the word used in Mark 1:19 for mending fishing nets, and it is a word for putting things in proper order. It is a repairing word. The picture is of something torn being brought back to usefulness. The way of doing it is 'in a spirit of gentleness,' prautes, the quality that Paul has just listed as fruit of the Spirit in 5:23. The tone of the person doing the restoring is part of the restoring. 'Watch yourself' uses a verb that means to look carefully, and it is in the singular, so that each person is addressed alone while the commands to carry are plural.

The two commands about weight use two different words. The 'burdens' of verse 2, baros, are heavy, crushing weights that a person cannot lift alone. The 'load' of verse 5, phortion, is the word for the pack a soldier or traveller carries, or the cargo a ship takes on. The first is what overwhelms, the second is what belongs to each person's own journey. The verb in verse 2 is a present imperative, 'keep carrying,' and the one in verse 5 is a future, a statement of what will be the case when each stands before God. The Greek therefore does not contradict itself, and the English difference between 'burden' and 'load' reflects a real difference.

The verb in verse 7 translated 'mocked' is a rare word that is built on the idea of turning up the nose at someone, a gesture of contempt. People can scorn God by living as though the consequences of sowing did not apply, but the sowing and reaping come anyway. Verse 8 gives the two outcomes: 'destruction,' a word often used for decay and ruin, and 'eternal life.' The phrase 'to please his flesh' and 'to please the Spirit' is literally 'into his own flesh' and 'into the Spirit,' so that the flesh and the Spirit are pictured as two fields into which seed is thrown.

In verse 9 the verb 'grow weary' is a compound that is also found in Luke 18:1 and 2 Thessalonians 3:13, where it appears with 'lose heart' and 'well-doing.' The phrase 'in due time' uses the word kairos, a fitting or appointed moment, and in verse 10 'as we have opportunity' uses the same word. The harvest has its season, and opportunities for good have theirs. The 'family of faith' in verse 10 is literally 'the household of the faith,' using the word for members of a household, and so the language of family comes out of the Greek.

typology.type: The law of Christ and Christ's bearing of burdens
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah says of the Servant that he bore our griefs and carried our sorrows, Isaiah 53:4, and Matthew applies this to Jesus' healings, Matthew 8:17. Paul now says that those who carry one another's burdens fulfil the law of Christ. The pattern is that the Master carried and the servants carry. The correspondence is real but it has a limit: Christ bore sin in a way no believer can, 1 Peter 2:24, so that believers carry one another's weight, not one another's guilt.

The Old Testament harvest is a regular picture of reward and judgment, and Jesus uses it for the final gathering in Matthew 13:30 and 13:39. Paul's own use in 1 Corinthians 15:36-44 compares the buried body to a seed that rises. The harvest of Galatians 6 therefore points to the end of the age, when what has been sown is reaped in full. The type is incomplete in that the seasons of earth bring harvests in a year, while this harvest waits for the last day.

Israel was called a household and a family, and the temple was God's house. In Christ the household is the church, in which all believers are fellow citizens and members of God's household, Ephesians 2:19, and God's house is the people themselves, 1 Timothy 3:15. The type is fulfilled in Christ, the Son over God's house, Hebrews 3:6. It falls short in that the old household was marked by descent, while the new one is made up of those born of the Spirit.

typology.type: Restoring the fallen and the Good Shepherd
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament pictures God as a shepherd who seeks the lost and binds up the injured, Ezekiel 34:16. Jesus says He has come to seek and to save what was lost, Luke 19:10, and tells of a shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine for the one, Luke 15:4-7. The gentle restoration of Galatians 6:1 carries that shepherd heart into the ordinary life of the church, though no member can be the shepherd in the sense in which Christ is.

study.christ:
The central phrase is the law of Christ, and Paul has chosen it to make a point about who stands behind the commands. The demands of the community are not an anonymous ethic but the way of a person, who has already carried what He asks His people to carry. When Paul says carry one another's burdens, he puts into a short sentence what Christ did on a larger scale. The Son of God took on our flesh, bore our griefs, and went to the cross carrying what we could not.

The passage also shows Christ's way of dealing with the fallen. The gentleness that Paul asks of the spiritual is the gentleness the Gospels show in Jesus, who did not break a bruised reed or snuff out a smouldering wick, Matthew 12:20. He restored Peter after a threefold denial, John 21:15-19, and He said that the Son of Man had come to seek and save the lost. In the church, restoring a person is a way of continuing His work.

The warning in verse 1 'watch yourself' is also a Christ-shaped warning. Jesus taught that those who see a speck in a brother's eye should first take the plank from their own, Matthew 7:3-5. The church that restores has first stood under the same judgment and the same grace. Paul's use of 'we' in verses 9 and 10 draws everyone into that one position.

The harvest of verse 8, eternal life, is Christ's own gift. Paul says elsewhere that the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord, Romans 6:23. Sowing to the Spirit is therefore not a way of earning that life but of living in the sphere where it has already begun. The cross which Paul will name in 6:14 is the place from which the whole harvest comes, since it is by Christ's death that the curse of the law is removed and the Spirit is given, Galatians 3:13-14.

We should be careful not to read every detail as a picture of Christ. The sowing language is a general moral principle, and the household is a metaphor for the church, not a code for Jesus. The links worth drawing are those the New Testament itself draws: the example of Christ's love in John 13:34, His bearing of our weakness in Romans 15:1-3, and His gift of life in Romans 6:23.
study.god:
The passage declares plainly that God is not to be mocked, and that statement carries a good deal of the doctrine of God. He sees. The moral order of the world is not an accident but an expression of His character, and no one can deceive Him about what they are sowing. He is the Judge before whom each person will give an account, Romans 14:12, and the passage treats that as a fixed fact that shapes the way people ought to live.

He is also the God who rewards. Verse 9 promises a harvest in due time, and verse 8 promises eternal life. Neither is an accident of nature; both are His gifts. The God who sees secret acts of well-doing does not let them be lost, and Paul says elsewhere that labour in the Lord is not in vain, 1 Corinthians 15:58. He is a faithful God, and His faithfulness gives the weary a reason to keep going.

He is the God who cares for the fallen. The fact that Paul commands a gentle restoration reveals that God does not discard those who stumble. This fits with the way He met Adam and Eve in the garden, Genesis 3:9, and the way He dealt with David and Peter after their falls. The gentleness he asks of His people is the gentleness He has shown to them.

He is the God who builds a household. The phrase 'the household of faith' suggests that God has gathered a family and makes Himself the Father of it, Galatians 4:6. At the same time, His care reaches beyond the household, since Paul says to do good to everyone. God sends His rain and sun on the just and the unjust, Matthew 5:45, and His people reflect that generosity.

For worship, the passage invites a sober reverence, since God is not mocked, together with a steady encouragement. Believers can give themselves to ordinary good works, knowing that the God who sees will bring the harvest. It also invites humility: those who restore others stand in the same need of mercy, and the God who gives us the Spirit is the God who enables us to carry one another.

crossReferences.note: Jesus gives a new commandment, to love one another as He has loved them, and says that this will mark them as His disciples. It is the source of what Paul calls the law of Christ, and it explains why carrying one another's burdens counts as fulfilling it.

The strong are to bear with the shortcomings of the weak and not please themselves, because even Christ did not please Himself. Paul bases burden bearing on the example of Christ, as he does in Galatians 6:2.

Paul says he is not outside the law of God but under the law of Christ. It is the only other place where the phrase appears, and it shows that Paul thought of life under Christ as a real obligation shaped by love and service.
Jesus gives steps for dealing with a brother who sins, aiming to win him back. It shows that restoration in the church is a task Christ Himself commanded, and that it begins privately and gently.
Someone who brings back a wanderer from the truth saves his soul from death and covers a multitude of sins. It stands beside Galatians 6:1 as a statement of how much restoring a person matters.

Jesus warns against judging a brother's speck while ignoring one's own plank. This echoes the 'watch yourself' of Galatians 6:1 and the self-examination of verse 4, and it shows that the one who restores must first look inward.

Paul applies the same sowing and reaping image to giving. Whoever sows sparingly reaps sparingly, and God is able to make all grace abound so that believers abound in every good work. It supports the generous reading of Galatians 6:6 and 6:9.

Paul sets two harvests side by side, the outcome of the things that shame and the fruit that leads to holiness and eternal life. It ends with wages of sin against the gift of God, and shows how Galatians 6:8 fits the doctrine of grace.

The prophet calls Israel to sow righteousness and reap the fruit of loving devotion, since it is time to seek the LORD. It shows that sowing language belonged to the prophets' call to repentance and not only to wisdom sayings.

The writer urges runners to throw off what hinders, and to consider Christ so that they will not grow weary and lose heart. It joins Galatians 6:9 in treating weariness as the danger of the long race, with Christ as the cure.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning, the Bible shows a world in which actions have consequences. In the garden, one act of distrust brought death and exile, and the following chapters trace how sin, sown in one generation, is reaped in the next. The wisdom books gather the pattern into proverbs. Yet the Bible also shows that the harvest is not left to nature alone. God steps into the story to change what will be reaped.

The cross is where that happens. Christ took the harvest of sin on Himself, so that those who belong to Him are no longer under the curse, Galatians 3:13. He sowed Himself like a grain of wheat that falls into the ground and dies, John 12:24, and the harvest is a multitude. This is what sits behind Paul's confidence that those who sow to the Spirit will reap eternal life. The sowing does not earn the life; it takes place within the field that Christ has made fertile.

The call to carry one another's burdens belongs to the new community that the gospel creates. Israel was meant to be a people who cared for the widow, the orphan and the foreigner, and the church is meant to fulfil what Israel was called to do, with a Spirit that Israel's prophets promised. The household of faith is the first fruits of a renewed humanity, and its care for outsiders is meant to show the world what the new creation will be like.

The story ends with a harvest. The weary who did not give up will reap, and those who sowed in tears will come back with shouts of joy, Psalm 126:5-6. In the new creation there is no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4, and the work of the Lord is not in vain. The small, unnoticed acts of restoring a brother, carrying a burden and sharing with a teacher are caught up in that final gathering, in which God Himself dwells with His people.

sermon.title: Sowing and Reaping (Galatians 6:1 to 10)
sermon.why: Keller draws out how the Spirit filled life shapes the community, in gentle restoration and burden bearing, and how the principle of sowing and reaping calls believers to keep sowing to the Spirit and doing good to all.

quiz.q: How should the spiritual restore someone caught in sin?

options.text: Gently, watching themselves lest they also be tempted.
options.note: Verse 1 calls for a spirit of gentleness and self awareness.

options.text: Harshly, to make an example of them.
options.note: Restoration is to be gentle, not harsh.

options.text: By ignoring the sin to keep the peace.
options.note: The goal is to restore, not to ignore the trespass.

options.text: By expelling them permanently.
options.note: The aim is gentle restoration, not permanent expulsion.

quiz.q: What does it mean to fulfill the law of Christ?

options.text: To carry one another's burdens in love.
options.note: Verse 2 links burden bearing to the law of Christ.

options.text: To keep the law of Moses perfectly.
options.note: The law of Christ is the law of love, not the Mosaic system.

options.text: To avoid all contact with the fallen.
options.note: The opposite; it means gently restoring and helping them.

options.text: To boast in one's own achievements.
options.note: Verse 4 warns against boastful comparison, not this.

quiz.q: What is the principle of sowing and reaping?

options.text: Whatever a person sows, to flesh or Spirit, he will reap in return.
options.note: Verses 7 and 8 state the sure law of the harvest.

options.text: That our choices have no real consequences.
options.note: The opposite; God is not mocked and the harvest is certain.

options.text: That only good people ever face any harvest.
options.note: Both kinds of sowing yield a harvest, destruction or life.

options.text: That God can be fooled by appearances.
options.note: God is not mocked; He sees and judges truly.

quiz.q: What does one reap who sows to please the Spirit?

options.text: Eternal life from the Spirit.
options.note: Verse 8 promises the harvest of eternal life.

options.text: Nothing of lasting value.
options.note: The harvest is eternal life, of the greatest value.

options.text: Only earthly comfort.
options.note: The promised reaping is eternal life, not merely comfort.

options.text: Destruction, the same as the flesh.
options.note: Destruction is the harvest of the flesh, not the Spirit.

quiz.q: To whom should believers do good?

options.text: To everyone, and especially to the family of faith.
options.note: Verse 10 sets the scope and the priority.

options.text: Only to fellow believers.
options.note: The good is to everyone, with special care for the household of faith.

options.text: Only to those who can repay them.
options.note: The call is to do good to all, not only to those who repay.

options.text: To no one, since good works do not matter.
options.note: Paul urges not growing weary in well-doing.

questions: Paul says to restore the fallen gently, watching yourself. How does remembering your own weakness change the way you approach someone else's failure?
Believers are to carry one another's heavy burdens. Whose burden could you help carry this week, and whose help might you need to receive?
God is not mocked; we reap what we sow. What are you currently sowing in your daily choices, and what harvest is it likely to bring?
Paul urges us not to grow weary in doing good. Where are you tired of doing good, and what would help you keep sowing to the Spirit?
We are to do good especially to the family of faith. How is your church family actually caring for its own, and what part could you play?

translationNotes.note: Burdens renders baros, a heavy, crushing weight to be shared; it is distinct from the load of verse 5, so the two verses are complementary rather than contradictory.
The law of Christ is the law of love that Christ taught and embodied, fulfilled as believers bear one another's burdens.
God is not to be mocked translates a phrase meaning God will not be treated with contempt or outwitted; the harvest matches the sowing with certainty.
